name: coldopen
text:
It's two in the morning. It's raining. And Wick can feel cold water soaking through his left boot. Again. He has four hours left on his shift, and every step squelches.

A lot of people think staying broke comes down to bad choices. Or not working hard enough. But Wick works fifty hours a week. So does Dee. Same job. Same pay. Same rain. Dee's feet are dry.

So here's a question. Wick buys ten dollar boots. Dee buys fifty dollar boots. Over ten years, who spends more on boots? Take a guess.

The answer explains why being poor costs more, why it isn't laziness, and how to get out. And the way out costs less than one pair of those cheap boots.

name: ch1
text:
The idea comes from a novel. In nineteen ninety three, the writer Terry Pratchett gave one of his characters, a city guard, a theory about boots. That guard earned thirty eight dollars a month.

Good leather boots cost fifty dollars. More than a whole month's pay. But they last about ten years. Cheap boots cost ten dollars. But they only last a season or two.

So when his boots fall apart, the guard can't find fifty dollars at once. Therefore he buys cheap ones again. And again. And again.

After ten years, he's spent a hundred dollars on boots. Twice what the rich guard paid. And his feet are still wet.

Here's the key. The poor guard isn't bad with money. The good boots aren't too expensive. They're too expensive all at once. That's the whole trap, and once you see it, you see it everywhere.

In real life, you pay this boots tax everywhere. Let's follow Wick and add up what being broke costs him.

name: ch2
text:
Tuesday. Wick buys a four dollar coffee. His account is three dollars short. The bank pays it anyway, then charges him a thirty five dollar fee. For a four dollar coffee.

Americans paid more than twelve billion dollars in these fees last year. And most of it came from a small group of people who get hit again and again. People like Wick.

Some people give up on banks completely. More than five million American households have no bank account at all. The most common reason? Not enough money for the minimum balance.

In March, the car breaks down. He needs three hundred dollars by Friday, or he can't get to work. A payday lender says yes. The fee is fifteen dollars for every hundred. That sounds small. Over a year, it works out to almost four hundred percent interest.

And most people can't pay it back in two weeks. So they borrow again to cover it. More than four out of five of these loans get rolled over or renewed. The fee keeps coming back.

At the store, the big pack of toilet paper is cheaper per roll. But it costs more today. So Wick buys the small one. Families with less money could save around eight percent a roll just by buying bigger packs. If they had the cash today.

Then a late payment hits his credit score. And a lower score makes everything cost more. Take the same thirty thousand dollar car. With great credit, the loan costs about three and a half thousand dollars in interest. With bad credit, more than eleven thousand.

Same car. Same job. Almost eight thousand dollars more. Add it all up, and being broke has a price. Dee pays none of it. Not because she works harder. Because she can afford the cheaper way.

name: ch3
text:
So why doesn't Wick just plan better? Why not budget, shop around, read the fine print? Here's the part most people miss.

In one well known study, researchers went to a shopping mall in New Jersey. They asked people to imagine their car needed a repair. For some, the repair cost one hundred fifty dollars. For others, fifteen hundred. Then everyone took a thinking test.

With the cheap repair, richer and poorer people scored about the same. With the expensive one, the poorer people's scores dropped. Just thinking about a money problem they couldn't solve made it harder to think.

Then the same team went to India and tested sugarcane farmers twice. Once right before harvest, when money was tight. And once right after, when they had just been paid. Same farmers. Same brains.

Before harvest, they did worse. After they got paid, they did better. The researchers compared the gap to losing a full night of sleep. Scientists still argue about how big this effect really is. But anyone who has been broke knows the feeling.

They call it a bandwidth tax. When money is short, worry takes up room in your head. You fight today's emergency, and next month's problem slips out of view. Wick isn't ignoring the fine print. He's just out of room.

It's not laziness. Six million Americans spent most of the year working or looking for work, and still ended up below the poverty line. It's a trap.

name: turn
text:
Here's how the trap works. No savings. Then something breaks. Therefore you pay the expensive way: a fee, a loan, the small pack. That leaves you with less. Therefore, still no savings. And round it goes.

It's not rare. More than a third of American adults couldn't cover a four hundred dollar emergency with cash. For them, every surprise gets the expensive fix, and the loop spins again.

But look at the loop one more time. It only keeps spinning because of one link. No cushion. Break that one link, and the whole thing slows down.

name: payoff
text:
Remember Dee? She isn't smarter than Wick. She doesn't work harder. She just had fifty dollars saved in a little jar when her boots wore out.

And it shows up in the numbers. A government survey found people with no emergency savings were almost nine times as likely to overdraft as people with plenty saved. Another study found people with a cushion spent about half as much time each week worrying about money.

So here's the way out, and it costs less than one pair of cheap boots. Ten dollars. Every week. That's five hundred and twenty dollars a year. Enough to cover that four hundred dollar emergency, with money left over.

The next time something breaks, Wick pays with cash. No fee. No loan. Just a receipt. And for the first time, the loop stops. His head gets a little quieter. And he can finally plan.

name: close
text:
So here's your first step. Tonight, open a separate savings account and name it boots. Set ten dollars to move in every week. If that's too much, start with five. A high yield account pays around four percent right now, so it even grows.

And the next time you buy something cheap, ask one question. Will I be buying this again next year? If the answer is yes, that's your boots.

Being poor isn't a character flaw. It's a price. And you can stop paying it, ten dollars at a time.
